fibre.does: Keeps your digestion regular, feeds the good bacteria in your gut and helps you feel full for longer.
fibre.why: Most Australians eat less than they need. Eating enough is linked to a lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and bowel cancer.

sugar.does: A quick source of energy. This total counts natural sugars in fruit and milk as well as added sugars.
sugar.why: Too much added sugar gives you energy without much else and is linked to weight gain and tooth decay. Sugar in whole fruit and plain dairy is less of a worry.
list: Check labels on sauces and cereals

saturatedFat.does: A type of fat found mostly in animal foods, butter, coconut oil and many baked and fried foods.
saturatedFat.why: Eating a lot of it raises LDL ("bad") cholesterol, which raises your risk of heart disease. Swapping it for unsaturated fats helps.
list: Olive or canola oil instead of butter
Lean meat with the fat trimmed

sodium.does: Sodium, mostly from salt, controls the fluid balance in your body and helps your nerves and muscles work.
sodium.why: Most of us eat far more than we need. Too much raises blood pressure, a major cause of heart disease and stroke.
list: Pick lower sodium options on labels
Herbs, spices and lemon for flavour
Go easy on sauces, stock and deli meats

vitamin_a_ug.does: Keeps your eyes working, especially in low light, and supports your immune system and skin.
vitamin_a_ug.why: Your body can’t make it from scratch, so it has to come from food.
list: Spinach and other dark leafy greens
Liver (a small amount goes a long way)

thiamin_mg.does: Helps turn the carbs you eat into energy and keeps your nerves working.
thiamin_mg.why: Your body stores very little, so you need some most days.
list: Wholegrain bread (Australian bread flour has thiamin added)

riboflavin_mg.does: Helps release energy from food and keeps your skin and eyes healthy.
riboflavin_mg.why: Your body doesn’t store much, so you need it regularly.

niacin_mg.does: Helps turn food into energy and supports your skin, nerves and digestion.
niacin_mg.why: Many of the enzymes your body uses every day need it to work.

vitamin_b6_mg.does: Helps your body use protein, make red blood cells and keep your nerves and immune system working.
vitamin_b6_mg.why: Your body can’t store much, so you need it regularly.

folate_ug.does: Helps your body make new cells, including red blood cells.
folate_ug.why: Especially important before and in early pregnancy, where it lowers the risk of neural tube defects like spina bifida.
list: Bread (Australian bread flour has folic acid added)

vitamin_b12_ug.does: Keeps your nerves healthy and helps make red blood cells.
vitamin_b12_ug.why: It’s found almost only in animal foods, so vegans and some vegetarians may need fortified foods or a supplement.

vitamin_c_mg.does: Helps heal wounds, makes collagen for your skin and joints, and helps you absorb iron from plant foods.
vitamin_c_mg.why: Your body can’t make or store it, so you need some every day.

vitamin_d_ug.does: Helps your body absorb calcium for strong bones and supports your muscles.
vitamin_d_ug.why: Most of it comes from sunlight on your skin, not food, so a low number here is normal. Talk to your GP if you’re worried about your levels.
list: Salmon, sardines and other oily fish
Mushrooms left in the sun or UV treated

vitamin_e_mg.does: An antioxidant that helps protect your cells from damage and supports your immune system.
vitamin_e_mg.why: Your body needs some fat to absorb it, so foods with healthy fats are the best sources.

vitamin_k_ug.does: Helps your blood clot properly and supports healthy bones.
vitamin_k_ug.why: If you take a blood thinner like warfarin, keep your vitamin K steady and check with your doctor before changing your diet.
list: Spinach, kale and other leafy greens

calcium_mg.does: Builds and keeps strong bones and teeth, and helps your muscles and heart work.
calcium_mg.why: If you don’t get enough from food, your body takes it from your bones.
list: Canned salmon or sardines with the bones

iron_mg.does: Carries oxygen around your body in your red blood cells.
iron_mg.why: Low iron can leave you tired and short of breath. People who have periods and people who eat little or no meat are more likely to run low.
list: Leafy greens (eat with vitamin C to absorb more)

magnesium_mg.does: Helps your muscles and nerves work, keeps your heartbeat steady and helps your body make energy.
magnesium_mg.why: It’s used in hundreds of processes in your body every day.

phosphorus_mg.does: Works with calcium to build bones and teeth, and helps your body make energy.
phosphorus_mg.why: Most people get plenty from everyday foods.

potassium_mg.does: Helps your nerves and muscles work and keeps your fluid balance and blood pressure in check.
potassium_mg.why: Getting more potassium, mostly from fruit and veg, can help balance out the effect of sodium on blood pressure.

zinc_mg.does: Supports your immune system, helps wounds heal and keeps your sense of taste and smell working.
zinc_mg.why: Your body doesn’t store zinc, so you need some regularly.

iodine_ug.does: Your thyroid uses it to make the hormones that control your metabolism.
iodine_ug.why: Especially important in pregnancy and breastfeeding, for the baby’s brain development.

selenium_ug.does: An antioxidant that helps protect your cells and helps your thyroid and immune system work.
selenium_ug.why: You only need a little, and too much can be harmful, so go easy on supplements.
list: Brazil nuts (one or two is plenty)

copper_mg.does: Helps make red blood cells, helps your body use iron and keeps your nerves and immune system healthy.
copper_mg.why: Most people get enough from a varied diet.

manganese_mg.does: Helps your body use carbs and protein and supports healthy bones.
manganese_mg.why: Most people get enough from a varied diet.

cholesterol_mg.does: A waxy fat your body makes itself and uses to build cells and make hormones.
cholesterol_mg.why: For most people, cholesterol in food affects blood cholesterol less than saturated fat does. That’s why there’s no daily target here.
